title: When DNA Evidence Outlasts the Statute of Limitations
hook: A crime can go unprosecuted forever once its statute of limitations runs out — even if DNA later identifies a suspect. Massachusetts is one of the last states moving to close that gap.
key_points: A statute of limitations sets a deadline after which a crime can no longer be prosecuted, meant to protect defendants from stale evidence and faded memories.
Massachusetts bars most adult rape prosecutions after 15 years, one of the strictest deadlines in the country; 47 other states already allow more time.
Modern DNA testing can identify a suspect years or decades after a crime — sometimes after the statute of limitations has already expired.
A bill signed by Gov. Maura Healey lets prosecutors file charges whenever a DNA match arrives, even beyond the 15-year window.
Legislators had tried this change since 2011; defense attorneys had resisted it over concerns about defendants' rights to a fair trial with decades-old evidence.
content_html: Every crime, in most U.S. states, comes with an expiration date: once the statute of limitations runs out, prosecutors can no longer file charges — no matter what evidence turns up later. The rule exists to protect defendants from being tried on stale evidence and witnesses' fading memories. But DNA technology has quietly strained that logic.
extra_html: Massachusetts has long had one of the country's strictest limits: most adult rape prosecutions had to be filed within 15 years, while ProPublica's Willoughby Mariano reports that 47 other states already give prosecutors more time. The gap matters because DNA testing can now identify a suspect years or even decades after a crime — sometimes well after a state's clock has already run out. A newly signed bill changes that calculus for Massachusetts: once a DNA match arrives, prosecutors can file charges regardless of how much time has passed. "Today, DNA evidence can provide new answers years later, and our laws should reflect that reality," Gov. Maura Healey said. The change wasn't quick — legislators had proposed it repeatedly since 2011, and defense attorneys pushed back each time, arguing that trying decades-old cases raises real fair-trial concerns as evidence degrades and memories fade. The episode is a clean example of how legislatures periodically have to reconcile an old legal rule with a new technology it never anticipated. (This card describes a Massachusetts state law specifically; statute-of-limitations rules vary widely by state and country.)

related.title: Due Process
related.hook: Due process is the promise that the state can't take your liberty or property on a whim — it must follow fair, known rules before it acts against you.

flashcards.prompt: What is a statute of limitations, and what is it meant to protect?
flashcards.back_html: A deadline after which a crime can no longer be prosecuted — meant to protect defendants from being tried on stale evidence or faded witness memories.

flashcards.prompt: Why did Massachusetts move to extend its rape-case statute of limitations?

choices.text: Modern DNA testing can identify suspects years after the old 15-year deadline had already passed
A court struck down the old law as unconstitutional
A new federal mandate required every state to match it

flashcards.explanation_html: DNA technology can name a suspect long after a crime — sometimes after the old deadline has already closed the door to prosecution.

flashcards.prompt: What concern did opponents raise about extending the deadline?

choices.text: Defendants' rights to a fair trial when evidence and witness memories are decades old
That DNA evidence is too unreliable to ever use in court
That prosecuting old cases would be too costly for the state

flashcards.explanation_html: Defense attorneys had resisted the change since lawmakers first tried it in 2011, citing fair-trial concerns as evidence ages.
